quiz.q: Which HTTP methods does the HTTP Caching policy cache by default?
quiz.explain: The default request caching condition is GET or HEAD. POST/PUT/PATCH insert or replace data, so every request is different.

quiz.q: With HTTP Caching on, a repeated request with the same key arrives within the TTL. What happens?
options: The app processes it again and updates the cache
The gateway returns the cached response; the request doesn't reach the app
quiz.explain: Cached responses are returned immediately without reaching the API's processing — which is why the flow's loggers appear only the first time.

quiz.q: You want `GET /resignedemployees?resignedDate=…` cached per date. What should the HTTP Caching Key be?
quiz.explain: The caching key extracts what to cache by; here the resignedDate query parameter, so each date has its own cached entry.

quiz.q: Entry Time To Live is set to 600. What does that mean?
options: A cached response is kept for 600 seconds (10 minutes)
quiz.explain: TTL is in seconds; after it the entry expires and the next request is processed again.

quiz.q: Your app runs on multiple workers and the cache should be shared across them. Which option do you tick?
quiz.explain: Distributed shares the cache across workers. Persistent means the cache survives redeploys and worker restarts.

quiz.q: Which response caching condition did the instructor suggest?
options: Cache all the default codes including 404 and 501
quiz.explain: The cache shouldn't hold error responses, so caching only 200 (success) is enough.

quiz.q: Which JWT origin option means the consumer sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`?
quiz.explain: Bearer authentication header reads the standard header; the class instead used a custom expression `#[attributes.headers['jwt']]`.

quiz.q: With RSA signing for JWT, what can the API gateway do with the public key?
quiz.explain: The authorization server signs with its private key; the public key can be shared with anyone and can only verify.

quiz.q: Why is JWKS advisable over pasting the public key manually?
options: If the auth server rotates its key, the gateway picks up the new public key from the URL automatically
Manual keys only work with HS256
quiz.explain: With a pasted key, all requests fail until someone updates it. JWKS downloads the key from the URL (cached, e.g. 60 min).

quiz.q: Which Auth0 application type was created for the JWT demo?
quiz.explain: Requests come from a server (mobile app → its web server → our API), so a Machine to Machine app with `grant_type: client_credentials` was used.

quiz.q: A request reaches the JWT-protected API without the `jwt` header. What does it get?
quiz.explain: The class saw 400 "JWT Token is required"; with the Auth0 access token in the header it returned 200.

quiz.q: On jwt.io, which payload claim holds the token's expiry?
quiz.explain: `exp` is expiry (epoch time); `iat` is issued-at, `iss` the issuer, `azp` the authorized party (client ID).

cards.back: Gateway stores the response for a request and replies from the cache for repeats — they don't reach the app.

cards.front: Which requests can HTTP Caching cache?
cards.back: GET (and HEAD). POST/PUT/PATCH change data, so each request is different.

cards.front: How do you check the caching policy works?
cards.back: The first request prints the flow's loggers; repeats within the TTL return from cache, so no logs appear in Runtime Manager.
Expression deciding what a cached entry is keyed by, e.g. `#[attributes.queryParams.empid]`. Default `#[attributes.requestPath]`.
How many entries are stored; when full a new one replaces another. Default 10,000 — you'd usually reduce it.
Seconds a cached response is kept (600 = 10 min). Generally kept within 24 hours.
Persistent survives redeploys and restarts; distributed shares the cache across multiple workers.
Cache only **200** responses; the cache shouldn't hold errors.
A small API returning DB host/port/user/password, with HTTP caching for 48 hours, so ~20 APIs fetch credentials once per 48 h despite quarterly password changes.

cards.front: Did HTTP caching work in class?
cards.back: No — loggers printed on every request; the instructor said he'd figure it out later.
Bearer authentication header (`Authorization: Bearer <token>`) or a custom expression — class used `#[attributes.headers['jwt']]`.
Symmetric: one key signs and verifies — less secure. RSA: private key signs, public key verifies — more secure.
The auth server signs with a private key; the gateway verifies with the public key, which can be shared safely and can't be used to sign.
JSON Web Key Set — a URL (e.g. `/.well-known/jwks.json`) publishing the public keys; the gateway downloads and caches them (class: 60 min TTL).

cards.front: Why JWKS rather than pasting the public key?
cards.back: Key rotation is picked up automatically; a pasted key breaks all requests until updated manually.
Okta-owned authorization server used in class to issue JWTs (Machine to Machine app, client credentials grant).
Header (`alg`, `typ`, `kid`), payload (`iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `scope`…), signature — Base64, dot-separated.
`iss`: issuer (tenant domain). `sub`: subject (client ID + `@clients`). `aud`: audience (domain + `/api/v2/`).
`iat`: issued at; `exp`: expiry (both epoch time). `gty`: grant type. `azp`: authorized party (client ID).
Gateway returns **400 Bad Request** "JWT Token is required".

cards.front: Mule API calling a JWT-protected API — token handling
cards.back: Get the token once and keep it in the Object Store or a cache for its lifetime — not a variable, which dies with each request.
Numeric timestamp used by the `iat` / `exp` claims.
